citation.title: LLMs outperform outsourced human coders on complex textual analysis

question: Whether generative large language models, used zero-shot, can replace outsourced human coders in reproducing expert (gold standard) annotations of Spanish news articles on five text-analysis tasks.
data: 210 Spanish-language news articles randomly sampled from a corpus of 24,134 articles (Factiva, 2011-2013) on Spanish municipalities and the Supplier Payment Program; average length 508 words. Gold standard by expert coders. LLM runs: 1,680 API calls (210 articles x 4 models x 2 calls), April-July 2024, plus August 2025 re-runs for two models. Human coders: 146 ESADE students (each read 3 articles, two responses per article, 420 responses per method).
method: Five tasks: T1 list municipalities (named-entity recognition), T2 count them, T3 is municipal management criticised (yes/no), T4 source of criticism, T5 target of criticism (single label from a fixed list). Four models (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet), zero-shot, temperature 0, two calls per article. Gold standard made by authors in a multi-step review with consensus on disagreements. Metrics: macro F1 (T1), mean absolute error (T2), accuracy (T3-T5; for T4/T5 a lenient rule counting any matching gold label as correct; 'unsure' counted as wrong). Also exact-match agreement against 70% threshold, permutation test for humans against chance, subgroup analysis by difficulty and length, prompt-sensitivity test, test-retest consistency, and a check for political bias in errors.

definitions.definition: Labels produced by highly skilled coders, built by author consensus, a first full coding by one author and independent second review.
definitions.quote: we define these gold standard labels as those produced by highly skilled coders

definitions.definition: A task in an article is difficult if at least two authors initially disagreed on the correct answer while the gold standard was made.
definitions.quote: a task in a given article is classified as difficult if at least two authors initially disagreed on the correct answer

definitions.definition: Word count above the 90th percentile of the 210-article sample.
definitions.quote: We define an article as “long” if its word count (as provided by Factiva) is larger than the \(90^{th}\) percentile

definitions.definition: A model performing a task it has received no explicit training for, relying on broad pre-trained knowledge rather than task-specific examples.
definitions.quote: zero-shot learning refers to a model’s ability to perform tasks for which it has received no explicit training

definitions.definition: Less specialised annotators, often recruited by crowdsourcing; here university students paid in course credit.
definitions.quote: outsource coding tasks to a large number of less specialized annotators, often through crowdsourcing

definitions.definition: Treating the second response as the true label and scoring the first response against it, for each article and task.
definitions.quote: we treat the second response as the true label and compute the performance metrics described in Section "Performance metrics", using the first response as the prediction

proxies.concept: quality of a classifier (LLM or human)
proxies.indicator: Agreement with expert gold standard labels: F1, MAE, accuracy, and exact-match rate against the 70% inter-coder agreement benchmark.
proxies.quote: applying the 70% benchmark commonly cited in the inter-coder agreement literature56, we find that outsourced human coders fall short of this threshold

proxies.indicator: Percentage of exact matches between second tagger and initial tagging.
proxies.quote: Inter-coder agreement—measured as the percentage of exact matches between the second tagger and the initial tagging—was consistently high across all tasks

proxies.concept: competence of human coders (not just poor effort)
proxies.indicator: Permutation test against chance (2,000 permutations), order-of-article fatigue analysis, and re-analysis restricted to above-median coders.
proxies.quote: the predicted values are permuted 2,000 times and the metric is computed for each permutation, generating a null distribution
proxies.page: Outsourced coders’ competence and task performance

proxies.indicator: Two independent API calls per article at temperature 0; agreement between the two; plus comparison across model versions over time.
proxies.quote: we issued two independent API calls per news article

proxies.indicator: Code 99 for LLMs, counted as incorrect; unsure was never used in the gold standard.

findings.claim: All four LLMs outperformed outsourced human coders on every task; Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored highest, often only marginally above GPT-4-turbo.
findings.quote: First, all LLMs outperform outsourced coders across all tasks.

findings.claim: By exact match against the gold standard (tasks T1-T3), humans fell below 70%, while GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet met or exceeded it, approaching expert-to-expert agreement.
findings.quote: the most advanced models from OpenAI (GPT-4) and Anthropic (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) meet or exceed it

findings.claim: Advanced LLMs also beat the above-median human coders; GPT-3.5-turbo was comparable to them.
findings.quote: their performance remained consistently below that of more advanced LLMs
findings.page: Analysis of high-performing outsourced human coders

findings.claim: Performance of all coders fell on difficult articles and long articles, but the better LLMs did better on difficult articles than humans did on easier ones.
findings.quote: more advanced models, such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4-turbo, generally perform better on the difficult tasks than outsourced human coders do on the easier ones

findings.claim: Adding instructions, clarifying notes and examples to the prompt gave no systematic improvement over zero-shot (tested on GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4-turbo only; authors call this preliminary).
findings.quote: this enriched prompt design produces no systematic improvement in performance, even for long or difficult articles

findings.claim: LLM consistency across repeated calls was high but not perfect and higher than humans'; a model's outputs shifted between dates and updates did not steadily improve results.
findings.quote: we find no evidence that within-model updates lead to steady improvements over time

findings.claim: Cost and speed: the full set of responses came back within minutes for a few US dollars per model.
findings.quote: We spent US$0.20 to obtain all answers from GPT-3.5 (April 2024), US$3.46 from GPT-4 (April 2024)

findings.claim: Agreement among the expert coders themselves was 83.8% for T1, 81.9% for T2, 91.4% for T3, 84.3% for T4 and T5 (72.7% for T4/T5 where criticism was present).
findings.quote: 83.8% for T1, 81.9% for T2, 91.4% for T3, and 84.3% for both T4 and T5

limitations.point: T4 and T5 were multi-label tasks simplified to a single label with a lenient scoring rule, which likely inflates performance for both LLMs and humans.
limitations.quote: we adopted a lenient evaluation rule that counted any overlap with the gold standard as correct

limitations.point: Reproducibility: identical prompts can give different outputs across runs or after provider-side model updates; authors call for tracking model versions and decoding parameters and for periodic re-evaluation.
limitations.quote: identical prompts can yield different outputs across runs or following provider-side model updates

limitations.point: No comparison with supervised models (fine-tuned BERT-type); relative performance is task, language and domain dependent.
limitations.quote: it does not benchmark against state-of-the-art SML models

limitations.point: Human comparison group was university students, not professional annotators or domain experts; hybrid human-LLM workflows were not tested.
limitations.quote: While this sample may not fully represent professional annotators such as policy researchers, journalists, or domain-trained crowd workers

limitations.point: LLMs carry reliability risks, especially hallucinations (confident but wrong output) on fine-grained, context-sensitive tasks, and opaque reasoning; only a preliminary check for political bias in errors was done (in an appendix, not read).
limitations.quote: most notably hallucinations (confident but incorrect outputs)

limitations.point: Gold standard was made by the authors themselves, with one author coding all 210 articles first and the reviewer seeing the initial label (not blind); the gold standard is therefore not fully independent of the study team.
limitations.quote: each article—along with its initial annotations—was independently reviewed either by a trained research assistant (RA) or by a second author

limitations.point: Task is classifying text of news articles, not organisations; sample is small (210 articles, about 1% of the source corpus), Spanish only, one topic. Transfer to organisation classification is not tested.
limitations.quote: Our final sample represents approximately 1% of the articles considered in19

limitations.point: Data available only on request; appendices and supplementary tables (Tables C and D, Appendices A-B) are not in the extracted text, so exact scores were not readable. Figures are images; numeric values were not available.
limitations.quote: The datasets used and/or analysed during the current study available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.
